transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-06-10
Time: 14:00 PT
Duration: ~58 min
Attendees: Lina Ortiz (Redwood AE), Marcus Chen (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (Redwood SA); Evan Kole (CTO), Maya Singh (Lead Infra), Derek Holt (Sec Ops), Rashmi Patel (SRE)

Summary (auto-gen may be rough):
- Deep technical session covering air-gapped artifact delivery, offline license activation, GPU driver/version compatibility, and runtime perf considerations (KV cache, batching, quantization) for on-prem Redwood Private deployment.
- Agreement to exchange artifacts (signed tarball + checksums), run local bench, and schedule dry-run install.

[00:00] Lina (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call then we can hand to Marcus for the deep dive.
[00:18] Evan (Starlit CTO): Hey Lina, thanks. We just want to make sure we get the install path nailed down — the security team is strict about any inbound connections.
[00:30] Marcus (Redwood SE): Totally understood. Today we want to cover two parallel tracks: artifact and licensing delivery for air-gapped installs, and then runtime ops notes — drivers, runtime deps, and perf knobs like KV cache, batching, and quantization profiles.
[00:48] Maya (Lead Infra): Quick note — our floor is radiator-cooled nodes with A100-SPs and two distinct racks; we'll supply inventory. No internet egress from the cluster.
[01:05] Marcus: Good. We'll talk through checksums and an offline manifest so you can verify artifact integrity without reaching out. We'll also sign the bundle with our internal GPG key and provide the public fingerprint.
[01:25] Derek (Sec Ops): We need provenance — can you provide SLSA-ish metadata or a signed SBOM? Security won't accept a tarball with no provenance.
[01:36] Priya (Redwood SA): Yes, we'll include an attestations.json with build IDs and a digest path. It's not full SLSAv3 right now, it's basic attestations but signed. We'll also include a short readme describing build environment and kernel module expectations.
[01:55] Rashmi (SRE): What's the recommended driver matrix? We had issues with cu d n n mismatches in past vendor installs.
[02:05] Marcus: We support CUDA 12.2 and 12.3 for the shipping runtime; preferred is 12.2. cuDNN must be 9.x series — we'll provide exact revisions. We'll include a driver-check script that detects the driver module (nvidia.ko) and nvidia-smi reported driver. There will be a small compatibility table in the bundle.
[02:30] Evan: Do you require a specific kernel? We're running 5.19 and one rack is on 6.1 for new firmware.
[02:37] Priya: Kernel 5.15+ is fine; 6.x is okay but we ask you to run the compatibility script. A couple of vendor-specific kernel configs (IOMMU and hugepages) improve perf; we'll document them.
[02:55] Derek: On the licensing side, how does offline activation happen? We can't accept outbound calls for license validation.
[03:05] Lina: We have an offline license flow: we generate a signed license blob tied to your account and hardware fingerprint. You POST the license artifact locally to the control plane. For full air-gap, we can do a manual key injection process — we'll provide a PKCS#7 signed license file and an enrollment script that takes the local node fingerprint.
[03:27] Maya: Fingerprint meaning MAC and serial plus a UUID?
[03:31] Marcus: We'll explain exactly what we compute: a combination of NIC MACs, system serials, and the TPM public key if available. If you don't want TPM, we fallback to a salt+serial pattern. The important part is it's non-replayable.
[03:50] Evan: What about KMS for model keys? We need to keep keys in our HSM.
[03:55] Priya: We support customer-managed KMS. For air-gapped installs, the control plane is offline but the serving runtime can be configured to talk to an on-prem HSM or a local KMS shim. We'll include examples for HashiWrap and PKCS#11.
[04:16] Derek: Ok. Can you also sign the artifact with a key we can pin?
[04:20] Marcus: Yes, we'll provide GPG signatures and also a signature bundle you can import into your keyring to verify everything.
[04:28] 
[04:30] (Transition to runtime perf)
[04:33] Marcus: Now on to runtime: KV cache behavior in an on-prem context. With large concurrent sessions you'll want a warm cache strategy — local persistent KV cache on NVMe speeds up prefix hits. We'll recommend a small persistent cache pool per GPU process to avoid repeated cold-start token costs.
[04:55] Rashmi: How do you implement eviction and size limits? We can't let the cache grow unbounded on nodes.
[05:02] Marcus: Our runtime exposes cache_size_mb and per-model prefix retention TTLs. We also support an LRU policy and pinning for hot prefixes. For privacy you can configure cache to not persist to disk (in-memory only). We'll include a config example: cache_size_mb=4096, prefix_ttl_hours=72 for high-traffic models.
[05:25] Evan: For batch sizes, our SLOs are 80ms p95. What's a realistic batch/latency tradeoff for A100-SP?
[05:34] Marcus: For single-turn gen at 512 tokens, we see ~20-40ms per token under good conditions. The batching window needs to be tight; we recommend async batching with max_batch_size=8 and batching_timeout_ms=8 for low latency. For throughput-oriented jobs set max_batch_size=32 and batching_timeout_ms=40. We'll send benchmark tables.
[05:58] Maya: Quantization — is int8 safe for our biomedical models? We need fidelity.
[06:04] Priya: Quantization profiles depend on model type and eval sets. For many transformer LM variants, we see small impact with per-channel int8 (QLoRA style) but we always suggest running an eval suite on your prompts. We'll include quantization candidate binaries and a small eval harness in the bundle.
[06:27] Rashmi: Are 4-bit options supported?
[06:30] Marcus: We support 4-bit quantization for some models but it is more brittle. For production-sensitive outputs in regulated workflows, we recommend int8 or mixed precision. Use our 'quality-monitor' with golden prompts to detect regressions post-quant.
[06:51] Evan: For the bench script, will it exercise KV cache, batching, and multi-stream workloads?
[06:57] Marcus: Yes — the bench sim has three modes: cold-start single-session, warm-cache multi-session, and max-throughput streaming. It outputs token/sec, p50/p95 latency, and memory pressure by process.
[07:14] Maya: How big is the runtime container? We have offline image caching limits.
[07:20] Marcus: Base image is ~3.5GB compressed; the full quantization toolchain adds another ~1.2GB. We'll provide an OCI tarball and instructions to load via podman/crane.
[07:32] Derek: About provisioning offline artifacts — what are the stages we should expect?
[07:36] Priya: Stage 1: artifact bundle (oci tar + scripts + attestations + checksums + GPG sig). Stage 2: offline license blob generation and key injection guide. Stage 3: bench script + runbook. Stage 4: optional driver pack if you need vendor-specific modules that we host for you (signed).
[07:58] Rashmi: Driver pack — do you ship nvidia driver binaries? We're vendor policy constrained on third-party drivers.
[08:06] Marcus: We can provide a signed driver pack for convenience, but recommended path is for you to procure drivers from the OEM and run our driver-check script. If policy allows, we can provide a driver reference tarball for ease-of-use; it's optional.
[08:23] Evan: If we use your driver pack, what's your liability on driver versions?
[08:27] Lina: Driver packs are provided as convenience and not a substitute for OEM support. We'll note versions and disclaimers in the bundle; final driver certification remains with the hardware vendor.
[08:40] 
[08:42] (Minor crosstalk)
[08:45] Maya: Do you need internet for initial image pull?
[08:48] Marcus: No, everything is packaged. We will provide OCI tar plus a small helper script to load into your registry or nodes.
[08:56] Rashmi: For debugging, do you ship symbolized logs or any crash dumps?
[09:02] Priya: We'll include a diagnostic collector that can be run locally which redacts keys and sensitive fields. The collector outputs a compressed archive you can share with Redwood Support via a secure channel if you choose.
[09:18] Derek: Audit logs — can we keep all audit logs in our SIEM?
[09:22] Marcus: Yes, logs are emitted to stdout/json and we provide Filebeat configs and an example Fluentd pipeline to forward to your SIEM. For the private control plane we offer an option to keep audit logs local-only.
[09:37] Evan: Rollouts — can we control model rollouts to a subset of nodes?
[09:41] Priya: Absolutely. The orchestration layer supports node labels and canary policies. In on-prem we map model versions to node-pools; you can do 10% canary and automatic rollback on error rates.
[09:55] Maya: Error rate alerts — do you ship rules?
[09:58] Marcus: We'll provide a starter set: token-error-rate > 1% triggers pager, and latency p95 > SLA triggers alerts. These are configurable.
[10:12] Evan: Back to security: will artifact attestation include package-level hashes? We need to prove binary integrity for audits.
[10:19] Priya: Yes, per-file SHA256 and a top-level manifest.json that lists every file and its hash. That manifest is signed with our GPG key. We'll also include an ocibundle.sig for the OCI tar.
[10:34] Rashmi: Any known corner cases for NVLink/peer access? We had NUMA imbalances previously.
[10:40] Marcus: We'll add a NUMA-aware placement doc. For A100-SP with NVLink, we enable nv_peer_mem and set CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES mapping in the runtime. We'll provide a tuning appendix for PCIe vs NVLink topologies.
[10:59] Maya: How long do you anticipate the dry-run install and the bench to take?
[11:03] Marcus: A basic dry-run install and driver verification is 90-120 minutes per rack for experienced infra. The bench run for full throughput across both racks may take 2-3 hours including data collection.
[11:17] Lina: Let's summarize action items and next steps real quick. Marcus, you'll produce the artifact bundle and bench script; Lina, I'll push the license docs; Maya you'll send the node inventory. Derek you'll confirm KMS pattern.
[11:29] Evan: Sounds good. Also please include the quick checklist for the security team — we need a one-pager.
[11:34] Priya: We'll attach a single-page checklist with the artifact bundle: items include signature verification steps, driver sanity checks, and SIEM forwarding sample.
[11:44] (Small interruptions — typing noises)
[11:47] Rashmi: One more question — if the quantization causes quality drift, is there an easy rollback?
[11:52] Marcus: Yes. Model versions are pinned and we keep previous model artifacts in the node cache. Rolling back is a single config flip or API call; we'll demonstrate in the dry-run.
[12:07] Lina: Great, we'll follow up with the bundle link (SFTP instructions) and the scheduled dry-run proposed windows. Thanks everyone.
[12:15] Evan: Thanks all.
[12:20] (Call ends)
